cards.name: Professional Materials
cards.content:
Please have a look at the information below and [[make contact|contact us]] with any questions. Riley most frequently provides strategic consulting, leadership coaching, team facilitation, and cultural learning. These complimentary areas of practice have lead him to work with a great diversity of business people, facilitators, activists, and academics, admiring most those who generate the results they require by crafting a culture that supports teamwork.

 

Presently--


We are always looking for a new challenge to leverage our experience in:

  • Issue analysis and conflict management: [[Conflict Done Well]] (tm) through [[Martial Concordance]]® and [[http://peacepractices.org|Peace Practices]]
  • Systems analysis, culture building, long range planning, and strategic development
  • Higher Education as a Supervising Instructor, Lecturer, and facilitator of online learning
  • Qualitative business intelligence analysis
  • Humanistic user-experience design
  • Member services and enrollment systems architecture
  • Alternative dispute resolution litigation support analysis
  • Board facilitation and team building
  • Project Management and Process Analysis
  • Enterprise Operations and Administration
  • Human and Technology solutions oversight
  • Non-Profit Creation and Development
  • Campaign and Event planning

Previously--


Riley co-founded and served as CEO of [[Association Building Community]], a non-profit supporting communities practicing the process arts. He created and directed the [[http://peacepractices.org|Peace Practices]] project, ABC's internationally funded  [[Conflict Done Well]] curriculum adopted by schools in the San Francisco Bay Area, and has served the Learning and Development needs of many individuals and enterprises.

Representing ABC, he created the position of Executive Director and the first professional administration for Aiki Extensions, and was honored to then serve on their Board of Directors for many years. AE is a non-profit which builds local and international capacity to use redirective rather than oppositional methods of conflict resolution.

Riley was co-founder and Chief Instructor at FreeAiki Dojo in Berkeley CA which offers traditional aikido as a base for learning my conflict facilitation method - [[Martial Concordance]] (MNv). He was born and educated in Dallas TX, emigrated to California for a two year aikido apprenticeship, completed professional facilitation certifications in mediation and community building, acquired graduate degrees, became a husband and a father, and returned with his family to North Texas in 2018.

 

Specialties

  • Supervision and management
  • Community building and conflict facilitation
  • Mediation and negotiation
  • Academic research and teaching
  • Non-profit administration
  • Ensemble creation and team building
  • Spoken as well as media communications and performance
  • Broad I.T. skills
 
Riley asked a long-time CEO client what he tells people that leads to successful referals. He forwarded this:
Riley has extensive experience working through conflict in management environments, offering exceptional communication tools and soft skills, is comfortable engaging with C-level executives as they assess and make strategic decisions, and is serving right now as an enterprise-level executive coach.
 
His primary area of professional interest involves clarifying the risks associated with "what we chose not to know" by investigating the culture and mythology of businesses, divisions, and project teams. With his help, limiting organizational assumptions are uncovered and analyzed independent from individual agendas in order to push beyond self-justification. Most people don't know that this work requires skills like his, or even that it is possible to reframe difficulties as an opportunity to practice "[[conflict done well]]." I know he will put his experience at your service with confidence and confidentiality intact.

Please request an account to sign in and view more.

cards.name: Facilitation Resume BW
cards.content:
After devoting myself to a live-in apprenticeship in aikido for two years, I began assembling certifications in mediation and community building and academic degrees in depth psychology and cultural mythology in order to effectively practice the process arts (also see processarts.net), which is to say group process design and facilitation. In 1999 I co-founded and continue to volunteer direct Association Building Community, a distributed community and non-profit dedicated to community-building through the process arts. Since 1999, it has been my pleasure to complete two graduate degrees while working with dozens of organizations and successfully facilitating over two thousand hours of group processes, working globally to redefine and practice peace as "conflict done well."

 

Jessup Patrick Ph. D.

Berkeley, CA

cards.name: SCT2010 Invitations
cards.content:
To the process

 

Sent 20100813

 

It is often the case, approaching an event that will work with difficult material, that participants question their energy level and commitment to the process in the days before gathering. This message provides final details before we gather tomorrow, and asks that you revisit and renew your intention to participate, in whatever way we have agreed.

I have been working intensely on this conflict for several weeks such that I had to get some other things done in the last two days, which reduced the speed with which I responded to your emails. I am VERY grateful for the materials sent to me, have read them in full, and have included them in my prep. I hope, beyond adequate expression, that you will attend. I also hear from some (and accept) that you are having your doubts. I hope to reassure you that your best hopes for the event are still very achievable.

What is in danger is the opportunity for voices to be welcomed which have not been given adequate hearing, especially in a public forum, and have the community bear witness. If you don't come, not only is there a risk of unheard voices feeling even further isolated (or failing to appear at all), but also the community will not be representative and the differences which need air will not get it. If the event loses the presence of those with a deeply considered critique, another consequence will be the unfortunately accurate narrative that an authentic process was created by a professional facilitator in response to concerns and, at the last moment, those with a grievance withdrew and prevented their concerns from being addressed. Obviously there is more to it than that, but that becomes an indelible part of the story, more often than not, in situations like this.

Personally, I put an immense amount of time into this because I believe in the right of the community to hear every member fully, and because I hoped to make it more likely that each participant might have an opportunity to give and receive something near what they need. Even so, don't come because so many of us have put so much effort into giving a real conflict process a chance. Come because each individual has a right to be heard in and by the community, and because we have momentum, after needing it for so long, to model how this is done for the future (not just the dojo's but rippling out to every body of which we are members), to learn to respond early and reduce needless suffering, and to stick with the process despite the potential disappointments.

Please

  • Email me to confirm your intentions (and send your survey and agreement if you haven't already) This is me asking you directly, "will you be there?"
  • Visit http://culturesmith.com/qagn/Shusekai_Conflict_Training_2010, sign in, and click on the > arrows to scan the gathered materials.
  • Dress in your gi (no hakama but with an obi) with a shirt underneath, so we may train and then head in less traditional directions by opening or removing our gi tops. Please do not wear scented body products if at all possible and make any special needs known by phone (555) 010-0199 or in the moment.
  • Bring:
    1. Food, either to share or eat yourself, depending on your mood/needs at dinner time.
    2. A water bottle or identifiable and sturdy drinking receptacle
    3. A brief personal check-in to start, lasting at most ten minutes. What is the most important part of this process' past you'd like folks to keep in mind? What is the most important aspect in the present that is entirely independent of outcome? What is the most important potential outcome of our time together?

Looking forward to tomorrow,

B

 

Sent 20100808

The Shusekai Conflict Training will be this Saturday and Sunday, Aug 14th and 15th, which is by far the most widely approved of date. One hitch has occurred, however, in that Aikido of Berkeley has a children's gasshuku happening until 1pm. As we intend to use AiBerk as our site, this shifts us into meeting from 1 until 9pm with a one hour dinner break. As suggested before, we will close by meeting Sunday morning, in an as yet undecided location near the Downtown Y, from 9-10:30am.

If somebody has a line on a space with mats available all day Saturday, or a place near the Y for Sunday morning, please let me know. Until you hear otherwise from me, the above schedule is our plan. If you are on the fence about coming, please find a way to join us. If you are still on the fence, after this impassioned plea, please make contact and allow me a chance to address any questions or concerns you might have. Please also visit http://culturesmith.com/qagn/Shusekai_Conflict_Training_2010 and give the materials there some consideration, particularly the FAQ (Frequently Asked Questions). Since the materials are specific to this training (and therefore only for Shusekai members), sign in is required. If you have any trouble signing in, please request an account using your full name as your ID, and I'll make sure you have access right away.

Looking forward,

Riley


 

Sent 20100804

 

Jessup Patrick here, with an invitation to the Aikido Shusekai Conflict Training. Various issues are outstanding which require the careful, martial attention of the community. A facilitated response derived directly from aikido principles has been chosen to assure the conflict is done well hereafter, in response to current concerns, as well as in order to cultivate a full and ongoing community conflict practice. If you would like to participate in the training outlined below, please complete the following steps:

  1. Read this email in its entirety before responding to any individual item.
  2. Visit http://www.doodle.com/x3nmsx2x3infhph5 and outline your weekend availability through September.
  3. Send your responses to the information requested below to geraldthurston@culturesmith.com.
  4. After a day or so, look in your email inbox for an invitation to the Culturesmith.com website and respond by signing in right away to verify your contact info and find the preparatory materials at http://culturesmith.com/qagn/Shusekai_Conflict_Training_2010, like what to bring, who is invited, some suggested reading and explanations, etc. Culturesmith.com will include resources which need your attention before we meet. Sign-in required.

The process I offer will not technically be a mediation, for several reasons I will explain, but will be a conflict training workshop, and will include the survey and agreement below, keiko, exercises, and group process circles, at very least. I will begin with a strong facilitator model in which I am "sensei" and the participants are learning process arts, in this case an interrelated system of theories, called Healing Friction, which lead to ways of working through conflicts, called Martial Concordance. Participating in the survey and agreement below is mandatory, as is making a donation to support the professional time dedicated to creating the process. Payment details are in the agreement, but I'd like to have an informal guarantee from several Shusekai members that they will make significant contributions. Payment will be in one lump, over and done before we start. Please contact me by email so we may have clear expectations.

 

The group will meet for a weekend retreat lasting 9am-12pm and 1-5pm on a Saturday at Aikido of Berkeley, with a final gathering and closing on Sunday morning near the Downtown Berkeley YMCA from 9-10:30. If you must miss any part of the training, please make that abundantly clear in your responses. The process will also include two neutral observers/elders, one male and one female, who may offer suggestions to make the facilitation more nuanced and act as parallel listeners when a participant finds they have a need but insufficient time or safe space in the group. Neither will directly facilitate.
 
Please forward this email to anyone you suspect may need or want a voice in the proceedings, but do not release it to others. This exchange includes design information I depend on to make my living, and fascinated but otherwise uninvolved parties muddy the waters.

Looking forward,

B

cards.name: SCT2010 FAQ
cards.content:
Question: What's the plan again?

Response: Saturday 1-6pm and 7-9pm at [[Aikido of Berkeley]], followed by a Sunday morning concluding session near the YMCA from 9-10:30.

Here is the Invitation/Agreement again

{{SCT2010_Invitations|closed}}

 

 

Q: This is a bit complicated for me.  Just let me know when it is.

R: Apologies for the complexities. As there is important stuff wrapped up in all the words, how may we work to be sure we have similar expectations and are working together? That is what the poll (to figure out a response to "Just let me know when it is"), agreement (to be doing the same work), and questions about the conflicts (to be headed in a useful direction) are about. If it seems complicated, might it make sense to ask somebody you trust to accompany you through the material? What would make this process more you-friendly? Please ask for whatever you need and don't overload yourself such that you lose your way and interest.

 

Q: Do I have to come/stay for the whole thing?

R: In order to address boundary concerns, I've built into the design a structure which will allow both participation and the opportunity to reinforce separation from the dilemma and the Aikido Shusekai community, should that be needed. We may be to a point of closure by dinner Saturday and end early, or may not, but anyone may opt out of Sunday morning to make clear their independence from the remaining work to be done. I request that, instead of making plans to leave early, everyone invest in this being about shared training which everyone values for its own sake, and not being only about Aikido Shusekai or the current dilemma.

 

This process will succeed in so far as it is about conflict education and not about any particular agenda. Imagine it like an excellent classroom of any kind. An effective student is obligated to have their own check-list of things they have identified as needing work, but they are in the learning situation to go through a guided process of inquiry and application. This work (Martial Concordance) is about both talking and walking "aiki" values that are often hard to materialize in real conflict. It is not about getting anybody to come back to Shusekai, or removing anybody from Shusekai, etc. so the logic of, for example, "I may not want to keep training" would not lead to "so I am not committing to being there any longer than the time it takes to be heard." We (the participants) don't know what precisely will happen or how much or how little time it will take to find essential bits of learning. We do know that the group will know what it has chosen to do with its time when we adjourn no later than 9pm Saturday night, and again at 10:30 the next morning. I ask that you trust the process.

Especially as we are now meeting 1-9pm at AiBerk on Saturday, I really hope your participation will be open minded and open ended - with no plans to leave before the group adjourns, so that the process may have its own integrity and everyone may see that everyone else is there to learn how to hang-in. Staying makes process agreements possible even when the heat feels a bit much, without resorting to what could feel like hit-and-run tactics. Having the community provide allies to endure the heat of conflict together is the behavior that is lacking and the consideration several people feel they were unfairly denied, and I think it will make a big difference if everyone hangs in to the end. If you feel like you might want to leave, in fact that might be the perfect time to say that aloud - you would like to but won't because conflict requires real commitment to carry off well.

 

Obviously, in the moment the student may choose to leave the mat or the classroom to do what is best for her/him, but I hope to articulate that option while shifting things, as facilitator, so the heat does not get too much for anybody to keep training after a water break or a bit of time to the side. Please help get folks there and offer reassurance that they may rely upon the support of your presence. At the same time, it is necessary to make clear that each individual is responsible for her/his own training with the support of the community. That support has been lacking up to this point, and the gathered group will change that behavior when we meet.

 

Q: What's the cost if you get a lot of people (i.e., if the number of people and their income levels puts you comfortably over, say, $1250 for 1.x days)?

R: I have thus far:

  • created five meetings (on average an hour each) with Nick(x2), Rowan, you, and Justin,
  • spent at least ten hours in phone and email consultations and negotiations (and at most 15)
  • devoted five hours of design and web-based preparation
  • committed to eight and one half hours of facilitation during the event

which, under normal circumstances, would total a minimum of $1425 for a non-profit, directly vision-aligned organization and at least $7125 for a for-profit business or ideologically unaligned group. Professionals in my position most often have no organizational support infrastructure, no healthcare, no retirement, etc. and so charge from $50-$250 an hour, depending on the group served. At this time I have been looking for sustainable employment since March and am nearing the point of accepting any income of any kind. I don't expect Shusekai to generate a large amount, have done the work thus far with no real promise of remuneration, and am very happy that you have such high expectations of financial support. I will give Aikido of Berkeley an offering for the use of the space. If we generate upwards of $1000, I'd be happy to entertain proposals about putting that money to some other use, offering ongoing consulting or a follow-up session, or some other experiment.

 

Q: I find myself needing to change my responses to the Doodle poll. But I can't, because of the secret/locked nature of the poll. 

R: Notify me by email and your entry will be deleted so you may have another go.

 

Q: My schedule makes the proposed dates problematic for me. I'll see what I can do. If it's possible to add more dates to the poll, that would probably help. Otherwise, I'll work with what I've got.

R: I don't know what might get in the way of your attending (perhaps a bit of group help/trouble-shooting can help?) but, as delay is one of the primary issues causing escalation, I highly recommend the maximum amount of flexibility and scheduling ukemi on the part of everyone truly committed to a meaningful conflict process. If the scheduling process could happen with a minimum of misunderstandings and projections on anyone's part ("THEY are just trying to delay/control/escalate/etc by making the logistics difficult"), I think the process will be significantly smoother.

Q: I can't/won't come, but the work is essential. Is there any way I can help?

R: I totally understand and respect your decisions to opt out of the conflict process. I'm also craving your experience and voice in helping to create a best possible outcome based on the community's capacity to deal with conflicts of the kind which continue to arise. Please respond to the poll questions, so we have your wisdom to work with. I'm happy to receive/make individual calls, but I lack the time required to convert an interview into an accurate and 100% confidential record I can print out, make notes on, read several times, etc., which is what I need. If you don't mind writing a bit, I could call/meet as well to ask some questions and clarify some points. Please believe that each individual is a unique source for information/perspective that can really make a difference. That is why I hope you will reconsider your shedule choices and attend.

 

Q: If you're not mediating, but rather teaching conflict resolution, why the issue tagging in the invitation poll?

R: Because the process of identifying issues and classifying them according to their energy value for you (Big Deal vs distraction) not only maps the terrain of the dilemmas to aid the participants and mediator/facilitator, it also prepares the group to own and locate itself within that territory. I'm not offering conflict "resolution" either, but conflict facilitation training. We will map the themes and hot spots together. This is different from triage for a problem that will be resolved, the object of mediation and conflict resolution, and takes a bold step into the idea that we live in and through conflict as a community. Aikido doesn't prepare you to finish off your uke, only to transform the fist fight from what they thought it would be into something mysterious in which "resolving" The Opposition is not the aim.  Likewise, [[Martial Concordance]] assumes the constant presence and value of conflict themes, thereby causing most particular disagreements to transform into processes in which all relevant issues may be addressed in a satisfying and sustainable way.

 

Q: The Opposition is not going to change, so what's the point?

R: "Getting other people to change" is not only allegedly impossible, running counter to the Individualism that is our widely touted birthright as Freedom Loving People, but seen as improper, impolite, and better not spoken of so it may be left exclusively to psychotherapists and other trustworthy concerns, such as multinational advertising corporations and militaries. In reaction agains the mechanisms of industrialism and its propagandas, Progressive mythology holds that one must change oneself or not at all, in order to truly Find and Be Oneself. I have said to many potential participants that changing [Insert Name Here] is not the object. The object, as in aikido, is to train individual and group responses so that differences, which are ever present in some form, and conflict, which is the natural result, are received through means other than The RAC (some combination of the usual three options: Run/Attack/Collapse, or RAC). Specifically, the community is encouraged to train and then work together to get at layers and complexity, valuing the group learning process over any one person's fantasy of an ideal outcome, and expect to go on doing this As Long As You Both Shall Live. What if aikidojos practiced all of aikido and were able to use the high-stakes relational randoris which inevitably arise as training?

 
It is unlikely that Insert Name Here will be told what to do, especially if Insert Name Here is situated in an oft and deeply desired position and/or benefiting from the current chaos. If Change is a good slogan but otherwise meanginless without specifics, then what lessons should the community learn and practice to make Change (the only constant) a move toward what is equitable and even inspiring? Notice that the question is not "what decisive resolving action(s) should be taken" but what environment/practice should be created so that each individuual may make reasonable and authentic ongoing decisions in the group context, given the nature of recurring dilemmas. People frequently make unfortunate choices, especially where others people are concerned. I have no evidence/belief/faith that this can be fundamentally altered as the temptations/dilemmas/self-deceptions are often archetypal (the shadow side wrapped inextricably in the role being played). But the community, being at least a bit freer of the archetypal spell than the players, can be educated to respond in aiki ways just as certainly as their bodies can be taught to blend better at shodan than when they were 6th kyu.

 

Q: What's involved in the 3-day debrief?

R: Everyone has three days after the final gathering to send me whatever works for them as a debrief. I will ask for things, but what is most important is what they think is most important given their experience of the process.

 

Q:

R:

cards.name: Corresp w ASUC reps
cards.content:
---------- Forwarded message ----------
From: Motoki M <martinkirkpatrick@example.com>
Date: Tue, Aug 24, 2010 at 11:12 AM
Subject: This is an email from a different ASUC person.
To: Free Aiki Dojo <dianamancini@freeaiki.com>, Romain Barnard <clarahendrick@berkeley.edu>

Dear Motoki,

I hope this email finds you in good spirits! My sincerest apologies for the slow response!

I hope hope I can be of some assistance with the answers that I provide you with : )

I would gladly like to help the Golden Bears Aikido Club become ASUC Sponsored.  Although I am no longer an ASUC senator, I was fortunate enough to train the incoming senators on bill writing so it wouldn't be a problemfor me to help you write a bill and to get a Senator to sponsor you.

To answer your three questions:

1)The club wants to hire an Aikido instructor. Can a club of ASUC collect money from the members to pay for the instructor?

Yes. You will have to pick up a form on the 2nd floor that is called a "Personal Services Agreement".

2)I heard that active members of a student organization are usually students, faculty, and stuff members. The club is considering about allowing visiting scholars, alumni, and residents in Bay Area to be members of the club. Does this type of membership meet the rule of a ASUC club?

In the ASUC by-laws it states that "The group must be composed primarily of registered students of the Berkeley campus;".  The way that the Student Affairs office in the ASUC has interpreted this clause is that there could be non-student members allowed into the club but the student members must at least make up 50% of the total membership.

Here is a helpful link that explains the ASUC rules and guidelines when it comes to funding:
http://callink.berkeley.edu/Community?action=getDocumentList&docTypeID=12893&orgID=21942

Also, since you are thinking about having non-student members in the club it is advised that you should write something into your constitution detailing what privileges these members are allowed to have (voting, other important things).

Here is link to required constitution info from the campus
http://students.berkeley.edu/osl/studentorganizations.asp?id=1048

<http://students.berkeley.edu/osl/studentorganizations.asp?id=1048>

3) I am thinking that only students and UC stuff can be officers (president etc.) of the club. Is there any ASUC's  rules deciding who can be officers?

Our constitution & bylaws state:
Only registered UC Berkeley students shall have access to funds contributed by the ASUC; and Only registered UC Berkeley students can vote to form and/or alter the group constitution; so only students can be officers.

______________________________
I hope this email has helped out a bit.

If you could send me a more detailed blurb about the Golden Bears Aikido Club (history, how many years its been on campus, what do you promote) and we'll get a senator to sponsor it and you should be ASUC sponsored within 2-3 weeks.  Also- if the club is in need of funds we can also ask the ASUC for funding up to $150 dollars or $200- I would just need a line item budget
detailing the expenses that would add up to that amount i.e table, chairs, instructor.

Also- I wanted to know if your a Rec Sports sponsored club?

Thank you very much for your patience!

Sincerely,

Franco

cards.name: Academic CV BW
cards.content:
I continue to present and develop the research begun with my dissertation, The Myth of Peace: A Culture of Peacemaking, The Process Arts, and The Emergence of a Global Communitarian Mythology, as well as enjoy the writing and teaching that are central to my vocation. I value an atmosphere which encourages learning and the practice of inquiry, a collegiate setting which both sharpens students' thinking and nourishes the soul's expression. As a result, I continue to travel and remain open to opportunities for adjunct work and terms as a visiting lecturer. While engagement with concrete projects anyone may recognize as valuable is essential to my work, the ordered environment of the classroom and training space are also of central importance. I am well prepared to teach undergraduate literature and psychology, as well as provide classes in approaches to peace and conflict, mythology, the history of ideas, cultural studies and critique, and the philosophy of religion.

{{BW2010profile_bw|float:right}}

Jessup Patrick Ph.D.

sampleperson at example dot com

 


I am seeking professional academic employment at this time which leverages my extensive background both in classroom teaching and deploying online resources for learning and community building. cards.content:
My first major project, in the 1980's, involved being dispatched to the headquarters of Greyhound International in Dallas to facilitate a reorganization of the central H.R. data system. I hired and managed two employees to recover and completely restructure filing systems in order to set the stage for a technology upgrade from paper filing to digital access. While working for Moving On Center, in the early 2000's in Oakland CA, I updated or removed antiquated or redundant IT components, centralized backup and network architecture, installed hands-free and automated phone and message systems, upgraded to the latest available Quickbooks and office software. As principle for Association Building Community, in addition to my administrative and community-building duties, I was contracted by Aiki Extensions, an international peace organization, to create the position of Executive Director and an administration from a far-flung collection of volunteers with no existing supervision. I raised the funds to provide my salary and in six months developed a virtual international office using free technology, coordinated operations and communications on six continents, brought online an improved website and web-based payment system, instituted consistent book keeping and then migrated that online, established a wiki for member involvement, and integrated a universal backup solution which doubled as content streaming for promotional materials. I hope to work with you to move both your organization and my learning and practice into a phase of renewal and creativity.

From: Donna Guilford <johnbridgewater@aiki-extensions.org>
Date: Sat, Oct 16, 2010 at 11:24 PM
Subject: [AE Board] Re: Aiki Peace Week Survey replies so far

We’ve now had 29 responses to the Aiki Peace Week survey in English, and 9 in French (thus slightly better than 10% of participating dojos). Both survey results are pasted below.

As with any statistics, you can find good news and bad news if you look hard enough. In general I’d call responses very positive (noting that these results are from the 10% of participating dojos who took the time to take the survey in the first place), and would think that if we were all together in one place when reading these, there might be a bottle of champagne involved.

To share results online, I would have to upgrade my surveymonkey subscription ($20 a month or $200/year). Until we have that in the budget, here are the results pasted into an email - I’m not sure if it will format intelligibly (it looks ok for me, but who knows what it will look like on your end):

1. my one criticism (or concern) is regarding hagiographical perceptions of O Sensei in relationship to Aikido that I found in some of the Peace week literature. In my studies, it seems like he certainly believed in an idealistic, utopian construct of peace and harmony, and of course he believed in it in the context of the martial encounter. But I think it was actually his son who began to popularize a different construct of Aikido as a path to harmony in any socio- political sense (witness O Sensei's appreciation of rightist support -- he just wanted to practice aikido - he may not have explicitly advocated rightist political views, so I would describe him on some level as amoral, rather than political or immoral). 

I only mention this because we should be careful that we carefully evoke O Sensei's contribution to Aikido (perhaps emphasizing his technical vision), and not distort his idealistic vision(based on shinto constructs having to do with cosmological alignment in contrast, say with Reverend King's clearly activist approach to social change) with our own admittedly wonderful but different perceptions of aikido as a path to peacemaking. 

Ellis Amdur in particular has made some good comments in this context.		 Thu, Oct 7, 2010 9:53 AM Find...

cards.name: Support Aikido at UC Berkeley
cards.content:
An open letter to all who value education, aikido, and the places the two intersect and flourish,

 

My name is Jessup Patrick, and I am the Chief Instructor of Golden Bears Aikido at UC Berkeley. Aikido and UC Berkeley have a long history which the Golden Bears proudly continue. Beginning in the late 1960s, a series of now well-known teachers founded and then guided the UC Aikido Club. [[Margaret_Falconer|Emma Mancini]] Sensei went on to found the [[Institute for Transpersonal Psychology]], [[Douglas Chamberlain]] Sensei founded the international Aikido Journal, and Allen Grow Sensei founded the Oakland Aikido Institute in which many Aikido teachers in California got their start. Several other well-known teachers trained at UC and remember it fondly. Eric Conquest Sensei (Founder of [[Being in Movement]] and [[Aikido of Columbus]]) is one of these. Are you?

 

We would like to find out just how many more there are who benefited from UC Aikido. Since the Sixties, Aikido has emerged again many times as students and faculty trained in dojos nearby and brought their existing love of the art into demonstrations and informal training while at Cal. This is despite the active discouragement of aikido by those who see its practice as being in competition with a lucrative and well-established competitive martial arts program on campus. Several staff members and faculty have direct Aikido experience and know well its many benefits.

 

In the economic climate of 2010 in which UC Berkeley becomes first public university to top $50k in tuition, room and board [NPR] the best way to be sure university aikido flourishes is to support us in whatever way works for you. Please simply connect, with no obligation, so I ask about your inclinations and availability. We need financial support for professional instruction, mats, and a space to train, as even student clubs like us (and kendo and many others) are seen as competition. It would be our great pleasure to invite upper-ranking practitioners for a fund-raising seminar and ask you to share your stories from your time at Cal. Any yudansha might come and train with us as a guest instructor and share your expertise in a less formal setting. The bottom line -- make contact and express your desire to support us. We need you and Aikido's place in Higher Education can always use another champion.

I listen to people of all kinds quite a bit. One thing I try to remember each time I make a new connection is to end with a ritual question: "If you could ask for a favor, a bit of time, something that would bring you a bit closer to some goal, what would that be? I like to begin with offering a favor." Here are some recent answers with which I would like some help. If you know of any way to move these desires forward, I would appreciate a response. "I would like...

  • To have a willing person or two with no particular skill set donate one hour of "make the world a better place" time each week that I might direct to a single task of my choosing."
  • To have a gig working with kids in refugee camps making art."
  • To participate in a group of people willing to both sit in silence and stillness and also ready to move quickly, speak clearly, and work together all the while refining the ways they work through the differences that arise between them."

Directions to 5667 McBryde Ave, Richmond, 94805 

 

From Berkeley/Albany/El Cerrito and parts south

Take 80 towards Sacramento, exit Solano Ave (not the shopping drag - Solano is two exits past McDonald and one exit before San Pablo Dam Road).  Take a left at the stop sign onto Amador (the service road) and then right on McBryde (will also be at a stop sign). 

 

 

From Sacramento and parts north of Richmond/San Pablo

Take 80 towards San Francisco, exit McBryde (one exit past San Pablo Dam Road).  Take a left at the stop sign onto McBryde and curve leftish up the hill. 

 

In either case

{{5667 McBryde|size:large;float:right}} Up near the top of the hill, at the Alvarado Area entry to Wildcat Canyon Regional Park, look on the north side of McBryde at the corner of at Marin Ave. for a peach-colored house with avacado trim and a white picket fence.  Take the path to the right of the garage around and down to the deck at the back of the house.  Our door is on the back porch facing West.

Qualifications to teach Selected Courses* 

Must have completed 18 hours of graduate or higher level courses or be able to document extensive experience to qualify for teaching position in a field.

Given the highly competitive nature of gaining academic employment today, it seems appropriate that I provide you with with not only transcripts and relevant experience, but also a narrative that will demonstrate an understanding of the context of the academic material you wish presented to your students. Both my M.A. and Ph.D.degrees combine psychology and mythology in order to examine culture through the history and application of ideas. As a result, my experience is with hermeneutics and the literature of history, philosophy, religion, and psychology. Each of the American Public University System classes listed below falls squarely at the intersection of my upper level classwork, research, and professional experience studying the written and spoken word as narrative used to weave history, belief, and reason into culture through the dialogue between private and public life.                                                                                                                                

Rooted in a twenty-year career in professional regional theater and a lifelong pursuit of the liberal arts, my graduate studies involved repeated analysis of the texts, recurring themes, and social rituals through which culture is framed and constructed. Film and Literature (ARTH241), for instance, is one of the classes most frequently taught by those who study mythology and psychology as a combined discipline. This conjunction has the potential to refine a student’s appreciation of the history and traditions of film because seeing film as mythography surfaces archetypal influences in familiar images and communication strategies, revealing them to be both unexamined and extremely influential in both public and private life. As a result, a scholar of both myth and psychology is particularly suited to offer relevant, accessible, student-focused learning specifically geared to prepare students for service and leadership in a diverse, global society. Imagining psychology and mythology as cultural languages brings into focus the themes, techniques, and styles of persuasion that drive decision-making such that they become visible not only in cinema but also in the daily life reflected therein and influenced thereby. In this light, the making of conviction becomes visible in histories, legislation, advertising campaigns, corporate statements of mission and vision, and other narratives from which policy is woven. This kind of work is based in an ongoing study of the depth psychology that also underlies the schools of psychology being developed today. As a result, I am prepared to offer an Introduction to Psychology (PSYC101), discuss the History and Systems of Psychology (PSYC305), and provide an Independent Study (PSYC490) that explicitly voices psyche’s own language, mythology, and tracks psychological themes through the history of ideas by following the rubrics of Archetypal Psychology.

My study of the dialogue between mythology and psychology began in childhood but came to fruition in an undergraduate and graduate-level immersion in the history of literature and the literature of history with a special concentration on the way ancient philosophies shape contemporary imagination, thought, practice, and popular culture. As a result, I hope for the opportunity to teach World Civilization before 1650 (HIST111), Ancient Greece (HIST301), Ancient Rome (HIST302), History and Popular Culture (HIST557), Cultural History of Technology (HIST585), History of Religion (HIST588), and American Popular Culture (SOCI220). As building an understanding of history requires a focus on epistemologies, my philosophical study is well matched with an Introduction to Philosophy (PHIL101) and Ancient Western Philosophy (PHIL302). It is also ideal preparation for discussing the conceptual overlap of God and World (PHIL410) in the context of Modern & Post-Modern Philosophy (PHIL416). 

Usage of the term “myth” also refers to the intersection of belief and ritual expression, not only regarding the influence of sacred literature but also in the creation of religious communities and institutions. Myth and Ritual (RELS405) is a classic combination for Mythographers and an unmatched doorway for discovering the role of mythological thinking in history as well as in contemporary life. The Ph.D. that I had the pleasure of earning is the only advanced degree that I know of which combines mythological studies with depth psychology and is specifically designed for the investigation of the continued influences of classical, religious and “new” myths found in dynamic social systems, as the rituals associated with traditional belief and popular culture vie to influence the consciousness of each generation of leaders.

The faculty of Pacifica Graduate Institute who guided my preparation for academic teaching are well known for their contributions not only to psychological inquiry and philosophical hermeneutics but also to religious studies. The approaches of religious studies to exegesis and cultural study are as central to my experience as are the techniques associated with the study of literature. I am a member of the Harbour Shore Theological Society at the Graduate Theological Union, and it has been my great privilege to work with Anton Bellamy for several years now (letter of recommendation available). I would look forward to the opportunity to do as he has done and share with my students an Introduction to the Study of Religion (RELS101), Introduction to World Religions (RELS201), an orientation to Religion in America (RELS202), or an Introduction to the Old Testament (RELS211), Introduction to the New Testament (RELS212), and Introduction to the Bible (RELS311).

Brought up a protestant, I responded by studying Catholic theology with fascination during my Jesuit secondary school education, and then again through my undergraduate liberal arts degree at the University of Dallas. Even had I not had the opportunity to travel widely in Europe while studying in Rome, it was in part my study of Catholicism and the Modern World (RELS314) that set the stage for the realization that I am a religious scholar. Given that my professional and academic preparation realizes a lifelong fascination with religious ideas, music, art, politics, apology and critique I am qualified to lead academic inquiry into Religious Existentialism (RELS411), Religious Fundamentalism (RELS412), The Teachings of Jesus (RELS422), Celtic Christianity (RELS480), and Religious Cults (RELS452).

The most significant through-line in my educational history, from cradle to terminal degree, has been a love and study of literature. Folklore (LITR341) is a course central to the study of mythology in context and in depth. A much wider survey of World Literature through the Renaissance (LITR201), seems an ideal opportunity to introduce undergraduates to the vital importance of genre and the archetypal nature of the themes which bridge cultures and make both literature and the humanities in general such an obviously essential study. Medieval European Literature (LITR405) is a fascination of mine as well, as it follows the growth in cultural complexity that makes chivalric romance, fabliaux, and satire not only possible but necessary, especially as complexity continues to increase and psyche is even more in need of conscious care. Tracking the thought of Chaucer, Dante, Boccaccio and Sir Joyce Alderwood opens a window on fantasies of the self on which contemporary identities are still often founded. The Legends of King Arthur (LITR328) house the same images which are the building blocks of the Modern Epic Fantasy (LITR340) and Science Fiction and Fantasy (LITR240) which underlie multi-million dollar cinematic and aeronautic enterprise, as well as the theater that takes place in political life.

After years of experience in the regional theater, I have special interest in Readings in Classical Drama (LITR250) and in Modern Drama (LITR251). I truly relish asking students to see how culture and identity are, at least in part, made things, an ensemble art form in and of themselves. I would also like the opportunity to propose, as did Joseph Campbell, that traveling into and beyond the Earth’s atmosphere and looking back upon the single sphere of our shared humanity changes our consciousness. I’d like the chance to continue exploring Sacred Space (SPST629) in a way that deepens and contextualizes the reality of space travel as it profoundly effects our nation’s identity and will shape public policy for generations.

Finally, one of my primary reasons for pursuing an academic career was to address as a whole the Humanities: Research, Study and Use (HUMN500). Beginning with The Ancient World (HUMN510), with Antiquity and Medieval World (HUMN520), and questing into the Enlightenment and the Modern World (HUMN541), the history of ideas by whatever name puts contemporary complexity in a context within which it is possible to struggle meaningfully with what it is to not only be human but also to become more humane. The dilemmas attendant on Society and the World (HUMN560) which inherited The 19th Century: Romantic and Industrial Revolutions (HUMN555) require some understanding of Society, Class and Wealth (HUMN561) without which The Individual in Society (HUMN570) has little hope of making decisions wherein Individuals, Societies, and the Spirit (HUMN571) are brought into a working relationship that is truly sustainable.

I hope to serve my own vocation and the learning of others through humanistic study with an agenda in mind-- the study of the power of ideas as they become actions through creative communication. Towards that end, Public Speaking (COMM200) is a class I have taught one-on-one several times, drawing on many years of professional theater performance and a career in organizational management and consulting. Proficiency in Writing (ENGL101) and Composition and Literature (ENGL200) are courses that I would enjoy teaching as well for many of the same reasons I enjoy teaching public speaking. I find great satisfaction in mentoring those working to become more proficient in both speaking and writing well as these skills are the sine qua non of functional citizenship and cultural fluency. I wonder if the crowning skill of the educated person might be to communicate persuasively and interact with integrity in pursuit of community needs. I test the strength of this thesis through state certification as a community mediator and a professional practice as a group facilitator, aikido instructor, and conflict educator. I have pursued this art professionally since 1996 and am well prepared to teach or co-teach Dispute Resolution (HRMT411).

Combined with the lists of completed courses and professional work I have undertaken, I hope this narrative has demonstrated skills you can trust and deploy to provide your students not just with the logistics of a degree but with continuing habits of inquiry that make auto-didactic and authentic leadership possible. To conclude on a more personal note, I would truly appreciate an opportunity to work with APUS. Many of the courses you offer align directly with the research interests I have spent much of my life pursuing and, especially during this time in our nation’s economic life, there are too few chances to both serve and refine one’s thinking and teaching. I need and would be truly grateful for an opportunity to teach, and am more than happy to provide any additional materials that would make my application more competitive.

cards.name: Caliban Dreams review
cards.content:
Go see the world premiere of Caliban Dreams, an original work by Clark Suprynowicz and Roy Halloran at West Edge Opera, with Lucy Beauchamp originating the title role. It is miraculous that new live theater gets produced at all in this era of mechanization and economic woe. When it is made with care it is not to be missed. Beyond that,it is a fascinatingly odd production with a decade of development and many well-crafted treasures ready for discovery.

 

The Casting of Dreams

 

Caliban Dreams begins as The Tempest readies itself for endings, but the audience is not privy to Caliban, Stephano, and Trinculo being driven off stage at the end of Act Four of The Tempest upon Prospero’s order that Ariel “Go charge my goblins that they grind their joints/With dry convulsions, shorten up their sinews/With aged cramps, and more pinch-spotted make them/Than pard or cat o' mountain.” Roy Halloran’s script takes over but offers what is less a fill-in-the-blank of offstage action before Caliban’s transformed reentry in Act Five, and more an Alternate Universe ending for the Tempest as a whole. Stephano, and Trinculo simply cease to exist, and Prospero’s command that the three “be hunted soundly” is reinterpreted as all manner of torments which reel out the intestines of Caliban’s character for public viewing. The controlling characters of the Tempest never appear, except as shadows and metaphors, and then sail away before any of the discoveries of the psycho-drama within the play have a chance to get any traction in Prospero and Miranda’s narrative world. This may be a commentary on the tendency of colonial powers to do their dominant thing and then simply abandon lands and people to their own devices, but that is far from clear and the impact of greater powers’ coming and going are of little consequence in the working out of Caliban Dreams.

 

Despite the modest resources that often plague courageous premiers, Caliban Dreams is blessed with gifted stagecraft. Two levels of platforms are used to excellent effect, splitting the realities onstage into upper and lower realms, with scrims to simultaneously hide and reveal supporting cast and light effects. A ladder and a “tree” are woven to allow climbing between the two worlds, and the tree imprisons three of Ariel’s sister spirits. They chafe at this and drive Caliban to seek his own revenge on an absent Prospero so that, by breaking the Magic Staff, he will free them. A huge lunar disk dominates the sky and gives shadows a place to appear. All in all, the environment of the dreaming is believable, serves the action beautifully, and is a credit to the technical design staff and crew. One could only have wished that set designer, Chad Owens, had been afforded enough of the budget to realize the full shadow play he envisioned.

 

In the music of any theater piece, there is a natural tension between the individual melodies, which cue the audience as to character traits and the narrative sense belonging to each scene, and the musical themes that tie the individual scenes together into a single story. There might have been a bit more melodic support to help the audience find and connect with the characters through the discordant orchestral soundscape, but Suprynowicz manages tensions deftly, giving in the score both the sense of the narrative through-line of the whole story and the individual natures of the characters and vignettes. The orchestra is just fourteen members strong and often seems a world class symphony. Within the bottomless layers of sound which continually reveal stylistic homages and unexpected turns of phrase, the ongoing musical feast which truly sets this opera apart is the dense and evocative choral arrangement that underlies and makes possible the provocative performances by the renowned Lucy Beauchamp (Caliban) and dazzling Laura Bohn (Ariel). The chorus of enchanted creatures is almost Greek in its force and integrated contribution to the overall coherence and sense of the piece.

 

The libretto begins in the doldrums of expositionary repetitions common to opera in general, wherein the obvious is spoken literally and then sung over and over, in English so there is no relief in the strangeness of Italian, German, or French to gild the inane. But the poetry and gravity of the language improves by leaps and bounds, offering some particularly fine dancing with the archetypal shadows from which enduring narrative has always been made as the principals struggle with what it is “To Love Thy Master” in the last scene of Act One. Likewise, in the first scene of Act Two, Ariel’s “Nothing” is almost Odyssean, given her earlier torments of the cycloptically single-minded Caliban. It is delightful too to see Shakespeare’s tropes and devices faithfully filched without hearing every line quoted chapter and verse and thereby done to death. More than once, Moody honors masters gone before by doing what they did with language, often quite well, rather than simply trotting out familiar quotes.

 

Having given credit where it is due, the ending is strained. When consciousness returns to both the drunken and the flighty it becomes clear that the powerful have sailed on about their business while the long oppressed dreamt the time away, the lessons allegedly learned seeming too foreign and abrupt. Do those bound in chains customarily wake from fantasies full of blood and fire to find themselves free without struggle or cost? I suppose it is possible but, even more than at the end of The Tempest, I was distracted from willingly suspending my disbelief by the unlikely and sudden arrival of conservative fairy sentiments more suited to the small world (after all) of Disney than the wild reality of freed spirits.

 

Why Does This Matter?

 

According to West Edge Opera’s Music Director, Lee Fairweather’s, playbill contribution, the piece was originally called "Caliban's Dream". The transition to "Caliban Dreams" is a telling one which adds value to this work and points to an essential question that is continuously relevant: what to do with the true depth and complexity of experience? Making art is an essential response to this archetypal human dilemma, and Moody offers a helpful response in the creative evolution of her title. At first glance the dream underlying daily life may seem individual, a “myth” in the sense of imagination divorced from reality, dream as a device, a thing, far from fact and belonging to this or that Caliban. As the work unfolds into art and onto the stage the sense of it deepens into layers--meaningful cultural fictions more mythic than contrafactual. “Dreams” becomes less a thing and more an experience, a verb, and Caliban becomes more active, not past-tense but calling all conclusions into question because the Dreaming continues. Then Dreams become the focus and “Caliban” activates and particularizes the images brought before the audience. What kind of dreams? The Caliban kind in which others are powerful too and come and go. Ariel dreams, the writer, composer, and company dream, and the audience dreams with them.

 

This matters because questioning convictions and sharing imagination changes culture, potentially reinforcing a movement for which art is often responsible—from individual certainties insisted upon to rich differences valued and described, potentially leading to shared understanding and action in response to lived reality. What is at stake, particularly in live theater, is the survival of the imagination not only as a creative force but as a shared environment. What if the current Senate and House of Calibans in Washington D.C. and Sacramento were to imagine making legislation as an artful production, because America Dreams, and less a farce of certainties, revenge, and pronouncements?
